citations.title: Aikido Altar: open-weight AI for sovereign security
excerpts: Written by [Selim Decamps](https://www.aikido.dev/team-members/selim-decamps) [Tiburce Gridello](https://www.aikido.dev/team-members/tiburce-gridello)

From 1.51 TB to 328 GB We achieved a total 78.2% model size reduction compared with GLM 5.3 at full precision, and a 32.8% reduction compared with GLM 5.3 with an AWQ INT4 quantization. Altar retains **168 of the original 256 routed experts** in each backbone expert layer, removing 88, or **34.4%** of them. The router still selects eight per token, now from the smaller bank.

citations.title: Opengrep SAST After One Year: Faster, Deterministic Static Analysis
excerpts: Written by [Dimitris Mostrous](https://www.aikido.dev/team-members/dimitris-mostrous) Published on: May 12, 2026

The fork allowed us to make several architectural decisions that would have been difficult inside the existing upstream project. First, we migrated the engine to OCaml 5 with shared-memory parallelism. At the time, Semgrep was still using a fork-based concurrency model, which made certain improvements such as Windows support extremely difficult. Moving to OCaml 5 established a better foundation for performance improvements and cross-platform support. As a result, we were able to introduce native Windows support. Then, we made cross-function taint analysis available in open source for the use of any third party vendor. In Opengrep it is available via the --taint-intrafile flag, including support for higher-order functions across multiple languages. We also expanded language support, adding Visual Basic, and enabling Apex and Elixir in the open-source engine. Clojure taint support was also added. Finally, the fork allowed us to remove telemetry and proprietary service dependencies.

basis.reasoning: The Altar post is by Selim Decamps, identified on his profile as Aikido Machine Lead Engineer, and details model-compression implementation. The Opengrep post is by its maintainer Dimitris Mostrous and describes substantive architectural and implementation work, including an OCaml 5 migration and shared-memory parallelism. Together these support a technical blog with at least two build-focused posts; confidence is medium because the second author is identified as a maintainer rather than given an explicit engineering job title.
